presentation: A 12-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of right knee pain and clicking without any history of trauma. On physical examination, knee extension was limited (range of motion, 20° to 135°), and the lateral McMurray test was positive. T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging of the knee demonstrated an enlarged lateral joint space and high signal intensity in the region of the lateral meniscus on both coronal and sagittal views. Diagnostic arthroscopy revealed an incomplete discoid lateral meniscus with inflammation and central vascularization.
reasoning_trace:
1. Consideration of a bucket-handle tear — “Because the MRI appearance of a double-layered meniscus is similar to bucket-handle tears and horizontal meniscal tears, it can be difficult to make a definitive diagnosis based on imaging alone.”  
2. Consideration of a horizontal meniscal tear accompanying a discoid meniscus — “A preliminary diagnosis of a horizontal tear accompanying the discoid meniscus could be considered. However, the arthroscopic examination revealed that it was a double-layered meniscus, not a tear.”  
3. Consideration of a discoid meniscus alone — “While the upper meniscus was in an incomplete discoid structure, whereas the lower meniscus was in a normal shape.”

presentation:
An 11-year-old Caucasian boy was referred for progressive swelling on the right side of the mandible. The swelling had been present for 18 months and had gradually enlarged; the patient reported intermittent tenderness but no pain. His medical history was unremarkable and there was no history of trauma. 

On extraoral examination, there was diffuse swelling from the right oral commissure to the angle of the mandible and from the oral commissure to the lower border of the jaw. The overlying skin and soft tissue appeared normal, and there was a pink-purplish area over the right upper lip. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

Intraorally, a firm, non-tender bony swelling of the right buccal cortex measured about 3–4 cm, extending from the right first premolar to the distal aspect of the right second molar. The overlying mucosa was normal, teeth were vital, non-mobile, and there was no paresthesia.

Cone-beam CT showed an expansile ill-defined mixed lesion from the mesial aspect of the right first premolar to the periapical region of the right first molar, with thinning and disruption of both buccal and lingual cortices, alveolar crest erosion, inferior displacement of the inferior alveolar canal, and root divergence of the second premolar and first molar without root resorption.

Noting a port-wine stain on the right upper lip and lumen-like radiolucencies in a radiopaque background, computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the neck with contrast was obtained. CTA revealed a 20 × 35 mm expansile mixed lytic lesion in the right mandibular body with no significant vascularity. Catheter angiography showed normal findings in the carotid arteries and jugular veins; reactive cervical lymph nodes were present. The CTA impression was intraosseous hemangioma (low flow), with other provisional diagnoses of fibrous dysplasia and osteoblastoma.
reasoning_trace:
1. Juvenile ossifying fibroma was included based on initial radiographic appearance — “Differential diagnosis included juvenile ossifying fibroma…”  
2. Central hemangioma (intraosseous hemangioma) was considered due to the port-wine stain and mixed radiographic pattern — “Based on the CTA impression, possibility of an intraosseous hemangioma (low flow) was considered.” It was excluded by the lack of bleeding during biopsy — “…which was additionally corroborated by the lack of hemorrhage observed throughout the incisional biopsy procedure.”  
3. Central odontogenic fibroma was part of the initial differential due to jaw lesion characteristics — “Differential diagnosis included … central odontogenic fibroma.”  
4. Fibrous dysplasia and osteoblastoma were provisional after CTA — “Other provisional diagnosis was fibrous dysplasia and osteoblastoma.” They were excluded when histology showed multinucleated giant cells and hemorrhage inconsistent with fibro-osseous lesions — “…eliminated the possibility of a definitive fibro-osseous diagnosis.”  
5. Neurofibroma, lymphangioma, soft tissue hemangioma, and vascular malformation were ruled out clinically by the firm bony consistency, intact mucosa, and absence of neurosensory deficits — “…did not support the likelihood of a diagnosis of neurofibroma, lymphangiomas, soft tissue hemangioma, or vascular malformation.”  
6. Hyperparathyroidism (brown tumor) was excluded with normal calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels — “The findings were within normal limits. Hyperparathyroidism was thus excluded as a diagnosis.”

presentation:
A 24-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with 6 months of fatigue and exertional palpitations and 8 days of chest pain. On examination, peripheral pulses were bounding and collapsing, and prominent carotid pulsations (Corrigan’s sign) were noted. Blood pressure was 110/40 mmHg in both arms. The cardiac apex was displaced laterally and hyperdynamic. A palpable diastolic thrill was present in the left parasternal area, and a high-pitched, loud pan-diastolic murmur was heard best at the left parasternal border when sitting and leaning forward.  
Electrocardiography showed left bundle branch block, left-axis deviation, left ventricular enlargement, and Q waves in the lateral leads, consistent with volume overload. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly with a left ventricular-type apex.  
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated left ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 20%) and global hypokinesia. In the parasternal long-axis view with color Doppler, there was a diastolic jet arising from the aortic root that dissected into a tract within the interventricular septum and entered the left ventricle. The parasternal short-axis view showed a multilobulated aneurysmal sac impinging on the lateral wall of the left ventricle and opening into its cavity. Continuous-wave Doppler measured a diastolic regurgitant jet from the aorta to the left ventricle with a pressure half-time of 179 ms, indicating severe aortic regurgitation.
reasoning_trace:
1. Infective endocarditis — considered as a cause of acute aortic regurgitation: “Differential diagnosis includes causes of AR like infective endocarditis of the aortic valve…”  
2. Blunt chest trauma — considered among noninfectious causes of regurgitation: “…blunt chest trauma…”  
3. Aortic aneurysm — raised by the presence of an aneurysmal structure: “…aortic aneurysm…”  
4. Aortic dissection — considered because of possible acute regurgitation: “…aortic dissection…”  
5. Coronary–cavernous fistula — a vascular communication mimicking regurgitant flow: “…coronary–cavernous fistula…”  
6. Interventricular septal abscess — an infective tract through the septum: “…and IVS abscess and are also close mimickers.”

presentation:
A 25-year-old healthy Malay man noted painless blurred vision in his right eye for 2 months after a trivial blunt injury. He smoked 4 pack-years, had no prior ocular or systemic disease, and no relevant family history. On exam, a right relative afferent pupillary defect was present. Best-corrected visual acuity was 3/60 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. Anterior segments were unremarkable bilaterally; intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg in each eye. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed multiple aneurysmal dilatations at the macula with loss of the foveolar reflex, 360° perivascular sheathing, and telangiectatic changes extending from the equator to the periphery; there were no venous tortuosity, hemorrhages, exudates, vitritis, retinitis, or choroiditis. The optic disc was pink with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4. The left fundus was normal.

Spectral-domain OCT of the right macula showed disorganization of inner retinal layers, thinning of the inner and outer nuclear layers, minimal intraretinal fluid, and an epiretinal membrane, with intact external limiting membrane, ellipsoid zone, and RPE; central subfield thickness was 266 μm. OCT angiography demonstrated aneurysms and loss of the juxtafoveal capillary network in the superficial, intermediate, and deep vascular plexuses. Fundus autofluorescence revealed a hypo-autofluorescent macular area with hyper-autofluorescent stippling. Fluorescein angiography of the right eye showed normal arm-to-retina and arterio-venous transit times; early images demonstrated aneurysmal dilatations predominantly at the posterior pole with an enlarged foveal avascular zone and a well-demarcated peripheral non-perfused zone with microaneurysms, shunts, and telangiectasia at the junction; late images showed leakage from aneurysms but no leakage from sheathed vessels or neovascularization. The left eye angiogram was unremarkable.

Systemic examination, including neurologic assessment, was normal; blood pressure was within normal limits. Laboratory tests—including CBC, peripheral smear, coagulation profile, fasting lipids, fasting glucose, complement levels, rheumatoid factor, ANA, ANCA, anti-β2 glycoprotein I, anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, RPR, tuberculin skin test, and interferon-γ release assay—were all normal or negative. Chest radiograph, echocardiography, carotid Doppler ultrasound, and CT angiography/venography of the brain showed no abnormalities.
reasoning_trace:
1. Tubercular retinal perivasculitis was considered, but excluded because “tubercular retinal perivasculitis is usually bilateral with presence of retinal hemorrhages, which was absent in this case. Furthermore, the Mantoux test and Tuberculosis-Quantiferon assay were also negative.”  
2. Syphilis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and ANCA-associated vasculitis were excluded on the basis that “Other infectious cause such as syphilis, and autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and ANCA-associated vasculitis were excluded from negative test results.”  
3. Behcet’s disease was deemed unlikely because “Behcet’s disease was unlikely too due to the lack of signs of inflammation in the anterior chamber and posterior segment, and is usually bilateral.”  
4. A prior retinal vein occlusion was considered but was unlikely as “the absence of retinal hemorrhages, collateral vessels at the disc, venous dilatation and tortuosity made this a less likely possibility… the arterio-venous transit time was not increased on FFA and hematological test results for possible underlying blood disorders such as sickle cell disease, polycythemia, and lymphoproliferative disorder, were within normal limits.”  
5. IRVAN syndrome was excluded given that “aneurysmal dilatations are usually larger and are mainly located at arterial bifurcations, with presence of neuroretinitis-like feature.”  
6. Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity were unlikely because “history was non-suggestive and there was no neovascularization, exudation or tractional membranes.”  
7. Unilateral atypical retinitis pigmentosa was improbable as “the absence of retinal pigmentary changes, largely intact outer retinal layers, and presence of perivascular sheathing make this diagnosis improbable in this case.”  
8. Idiopathic Coats’ disease and Leber’s miliary aneurysms were considered but found unconvincing since “this diagnosis falls short due to the absence of typical exudation and the presence of peripheral perivascular sheathing which is indicative of an inflammatory component.”

presentation:
A 12-year-old Caucasian Italian boy was evaluated for dental anomalies. His parents noted feeding difficulties during infancy and mild developmental delay. On examination, his stature and weight were below the third percentile, and head circumference was small. Facial features included frontal bossing, low-set ears, a saddle-shaped nose, triangular face, palpebral ptosis, hypertelorism, and micrognathia. Multiple nevi were present on the skin. His voice was high-pitched, and he had mild cognitive impairment. 

Laboratory studies—complete blood count, serum chemistry, thyroid function tests, sweat chloride test, and chromosomal analysis—were all within normal limits. His surgical history included repair of a cleft palate and cataract extraction. Cardiac evaluation revealed small atrial and ventricular septal defects. Lumbar spine radiographs showed a right-convex scoliosis. 

Oral examination revealed absence of both the lower and upper right canines, delayed eruption and rotation of the lower incisors due to incipient caries, and a high, narrow palate. Hand and wrist radiographs demonstrated that bone age corresponded to chronological age. A panoramic radiograph showed chronologically delayed eruption and radicular abnormalities of the second molars. Anteroposterior skull imaging revealed hypoplastic frontal sinuses and mild nasal septal deviation. Lateral skull radiographs demonstrated a skeletal class II relationship, ethmoid cell hypoplasia, increased frontal bone thickness, normal maxillary sinuses, and mild hyperostosis frontalis.
reasoning_trace:
1. Bloom syndrome was considered because of growth failure and microcephaly but was excluded by normal chromosomal analysis and the absence of hyper-recombination: “Laboratory studies…chromosomal analysis, which had all given normal results.”; “BS is the only disorder in which such evidence of hyper-recombination is known to occur.”  
2. Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome was considered due to overlapping facial and growth features linked to a cholesterol biosynthesis defect but was excluded by normal chemistry tests: “chemistry tests...all gave normal results.”; “Recently, a case of DS with persistently low cholesterol levels has been described.”  
3. Fetal alcohol syndrome was considered because of phenotypic overlap but was distinguished by the genetic inheritance pattern and lack of maternal alcohol‐exposure markers: “the symptoms that are expressed are very similar to fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), and further studies need to be performed…”; “no genetic markers have yet been found, except in mouse models.”

presentation: A 38-year-old man presented with a one-month history of back pain radiating to the right flank and abdomen that had recently worsened. He sustained a C5-6 spinal cord injury 20 years earlier and had been bedridden since, with intermittent back pain over the past 10 years. Clinical examination revealed complete, flaccid, areflexic paralysis of both lower limbs and loss of sensation below T2. There was limitation of motion at the right hip without contractures; no palpable masses, fluid collections, or lymphadenopathy were noted. Laboratory analysis revealed no signs of a spinal infection. Plain radiographs showed erosion and destruction of the L5 vertebral body and sacrum, with paravertebral hypertrophic ossification forming a pseudotumoral mass around the L5–S1 joint. Three-dimensional CT highlighted severe intervertebral dislocation at L5–S1. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an osteolytic lesion at L5 and S1 with peripheral and paravertebral gadolinium enhancement.
reasoning_trace:
1. Chronic spinal infection was considered given the destructive radiographic appearance — “In view of these radiological features, the possibility of a chronic infection … was envisaged, and this prompted us to perform a vertebral needle biopsy.”  
2. A cancerous (neoplastic) process was considered because of the osteolytic lesion with a pseudotumoral ossification — “In view of these radiological features, … a cancerous process was envisaged, and this prompted us to perform a vertebral needle biopsy.”  
3. Charcot spinal arthropathy was diagnosed based on the patient’s history of impaired spinal sensation, massive bone destruction with new bone formation on imaging, and chronic fibrotic changes on histology — “Based on clinical history, laboratory finding, and histologic features the lesion was consistent with CSA.”

presentation:
A 37-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of a rapidly enlarging mass on the left first toe. He denied trauma or infection; a prior dermatologist had treated the lesion as a viral wart without improvement. On examination, there was a 9.5×8 cm polypoid, necrotic mass with irregular margins, ulceration, and intermittent bleeding. Ambulation was limited by pain and tumor bulk. Radiographs of the foot showed no bony involvement. There was no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy, and ultrasound of the groin was normal. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. The patient underwent wide local excision, which was extended to amputation of the toe to achieve clear margins. 
Histological examination of the excised specimen revealed a tumor in the dermis and subcutis composed of cohesive sheets and trabeculae of uniform small to medium round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, scant pale cytoplasm, indistinct borders, prominent mitotic activity (30–35 mitoses per 10 high-power fields), a Ki-67 index of approximately 80%, numerous apoptotic cells, focal rosette formation, lobulated growth separated by fibrovascular septa, and extensive necrosis and hemorrhage. The overlying epidermis was ulcerated, and the lesion infiltrated deep margins without bone involvement.
reasoning_trace:
1. Rhabdomyosarcoma was excluded by lack of muscle-lineage markers — “the distinction was possible by absence of staining for specific immunohistochemical markers such as actin, desmin …”  
2. Melanoma was excluded by absence of melanocytic markers — “… such as … S100, HMB45 …”  
3. Carcinoma (including Merkel cell) was excluded by lack of epithelial/neuroendocrine markers — “… such as … CK20, synaptophisin, chromogranin …”  
4. Poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma was excluded by negative TLE-1 staining — “… such as … TLE-1 …”  
5. Lymphoma was excluded by absence of lymphoid markers — “… such as … Tdt, CD20 and CD3.”  
6. Ewing sarcoma was supported by CD99 expression — “was immunohistochemically positive for CD99 in a characteristic membrane pattern”  
7. The specific t(11;22) translocation confirmed the diagnosis — “molecular results shows t(11;22 translocation) involving gene EWRS1.”

presentation:
A 27-year-old nulliparous Japanese woman with a history of infantile epilepsy presented at 13 weeks of gestation. She resumed antiepileptic therapy at age 17 and, without preconception counseling, continued her pregnancy while taking valproate 1400 mg/day, phenobarbital 140 mg/day, and carbamazepine 1200 mg/day. Drug levels at 13 weeks were within therapeutic ranges: valproate 80 μg/ml, phenobarbital 26.1 μg/ml, and carbamazepine 10.5 μg/ml. Despite therapy, she experienced three convulsions per week. She took folic acid 5 mg/day.  
Second-trimester ultrasound at 20 weeks was limited by maternal obesity (BMI 30 kg/m2) and showed no anomalies. At 25 weeks, transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated contracture of the fetal right wrist joint suggesting a radial ray defect. From 32 weeks onward, the fetus exhibited growth retardation.  
At 34 weeks, estimated fetal weight was 1660 g (−2.5 SD), biparietal diameter 74.9 mm (−2.8 SD), abdominal circumference 261.7 mm (−1.5 SD), femur length 58 mm (−1.3 SD), right ulna 35 mm (−8.4 SD) versus left ulna 53 mm (−1.1 SD), and no right radial ray was detected.  
At 37 weeks, three-dimensional ultrasonography revealed a saddle nose deformity.  
On the basis of the right radial ray defect and saddle nose, a syndromic diagnosis was suspected.
reasoning_trace:
1. Trisomy 18 — “micrognathia (trisomy 18, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, acrofacial dysostosis, Baller-Gerold syndrome, and TAR (thrombocytopenia with absent radius) syndrome)”  
2. Trisomy 13 — “cleft lip and/or palate (trisomy 13, Roberts syndrome, and Aase syndrome)”  
3. Cornelia de Lange syndrome — “micrognathia (trisomy 18, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, …) … mandibular protrusion (Cornelia de Lange syndrome)”  
4. Roberts syndrome — “cleft lip and/or palate (trisomy 13, Roberts syndrome, and Aase syndrome)”  
5. Acrofacial dysostosis — “micrognathia (… acrofacial dysostosis …)”  
6. Baller-Gerold syndrome — “micrognathia (… Baller-Gerold syndrome …)”  
7. Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome — “micrognathia (… TAR (thrombocytopenia with absent radius) syndrome)”  
8. Fanconi anemia — “microphthalmus (Fanconi anemia)”  
9. Aase syndrome — “cleft lip and/or palate (… Aase syndrome)”  
10. Holt-Oram syndrome — “hypertelorism (Holt-Oram syndrome)”  
11. VACTERL association — “VACTERL association … is associated with radial ray defects, but it is not usually accompanied by facial anomaly”  
12. Binder syndrome — “Binder syndrome is characterized by a flat midface and nasal hypoplasia, it is not usually accompanied by radial ray defects”

presentation: A 46-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 2-year history of right hemifacial spasm. She had normal development, no history of malignancy, severe head injury, or family neurological disease. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable except for right hemifacial spasm with synkinesis. A non-contrast head CT revealed a 6 mm intraosseous defect in the right occipital bone. Heavily T2-weighted MR cisternography showed a 6 mm isointense mass outside the right cerebellar hemisphere, corresponding to the bone defect. A rim of high-intensity signal consistent with cerebrospinal fluid surrounded the mass and was continuous with the intracranial subarachnoid space.
reasoning_trace:
1. Chiari malformation (tonsillar herniation) — “these cases should be referred to as displacement of the cerebellum, and not ectopia.”  
2. Cerebellar heterotopia (cortical dysplasia) — “ectopic cells occur outside their organ of origin whereas heterotopic cells are in an aberrant location within their organ of origin.”  
3. Neural tube defect–associated herniation — “Four of these cases were associated with neural tube defects.”  
4. Nasopharyngeal teratoma with cerebellar tissue — “two cases involved nasopharyngeal teratoma with ectopic cerebellar tissue in the suprasellar region.”  
5. Primary diffuse leptomeningeal gliomatosis — “primary diffuse leptomeningeal gliomatosis can arise from ectopic glial tissue…often associated with progressive deterioration of clinical status.”  
6. Malignant glioma arising from ectopic glial tissue — “A rare case of malignant glioma suspected to have arisen from ectopic glial tissue at the cavernous sinus has also been reported.”  
7. Intraosseous skull neoplasms (meningioma, hemangioma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, dermoid cyst, multiple myeloma, malignant lymphoma) — “An intraosseous osteolytic lesion of the skull…needs to be distinguished from intraosseous neoplasms, such as meningioma, hemangioma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, dermoid cyst, multiple myeloma, and malignant lymphoma.”

presentation:
A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with a 9-month history of progressive swelling in the left parotid region. On examination, a soft, non-tender mass was palpable in the left parotid gland. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed an irregularly shaped, well-circumscribed mass with a low-density central area in the left parotid gland. The patient underwent partial parotidectomy under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, a 3.0 × 2.0 cm soft, cystic mass was located deep in the parotid lobe, immediately beneath the buccal branch of the facial nerve; there was no facial nerve weakness postoperatively.  
Gross histologic examination demonstrated closely packed ductal structures in close contact with a unilocular cystic space, both components showing a double-layered arrangement. The luminal cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm, and the outer layer comprised basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm. Secondary stromal fibrosis was present, and no definitive fibrous capsule separating the lesion from surrounding parotid parenchyma or fat was identified. In areas of the lesion, diastase-resistant PAS-positive inclusions were observed on the luminal surfaces of the ducts, and a direct transitional zone was seen between native acinar units and the proliferating small ducts.
reasoning_trace:
1. Basal cell adenoma — “These findings were reminiscent of basal cell adenoma or basal cell adenocarcinoma” but excluded because “a definitive fibrous capsule between the lesion and the surrounding fatty tissue or the parotid parenchyma was not observed.”  
2. Basal cell adenocarcinoma — considered due to the absence of a capsule and basaloid architecture, as “it frequently lacks a capsular structure, thereby mimicking basal cell adenocarcinoma,” but excluded by the absence of invasive growth and preserved ductal-myoepithelial architecture.  
3. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma — previously linked to similar intercalated duct lesions, as “Di Palma and Chetty … suggested the presence of a close relationship between these lesions and epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma,” but excluded by the identification of PAS-positive zymogen granules indicating acinar origin.  
4. Intercalated duct hyperplasia — once designated in similar lesions in the WHO classification, but excluded because “intercalated duct hyperplasia is not always the proper designation, and this is the reason why we prefer the term ADP/H,” reflecting that the lesion arises from acinar atrophy and ductal proliferation rather than preexisting intercalated duct expansion.

presentation:
A 34-year-old woman with a smoking history and a past history of asthma, nasal polyps, and sinusitis presented with sudden severe chest pain followed by ventricular fibrillation. After successful resuscitation, her consciousness and vital signs were normal. Cardiac enzymes were elevated (CK-MB 7.1 ng/mL [<5.0 ng/mL]; troponin I 0.23 ng/mL [<0.028 ng/mL]). ECG showed right ventricular hypertrophy without ischaemic changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular function, right ventricular dilatation, tricuspid regurgitation with a peak gradient of 61 mmHg, and an RV fractional area change of 16.5%. Emergent contrast-enhanced CT excluded pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection. Urgent right heart catheterization revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 66 mmHg, indicating severe pulmonary hypertension. 

During hospitalization, she experienced recurrent chest pains despite therapy with benidipine, nicorandil, and nitrates; ECG during episodes showed ST-segment elevation in leads I and aVL, large T waves in V3–V6, and ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. She also developed severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ 92% on 10 L/min O₂) that did not improve after two weeks of high-dose inhaled corticosteroids. 

On transfer to our center, examination revealed an accentuated second heart sound but was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed troponin T 0.244 ng/mL (<0.1 ng/mL) and marked hypereosinophilia (2.0 × 10⁹/L; 17% of leukocytes). ANCA tests and specific IgE for Aspergillus were negative on two occasions. Stool studies for parasites were negative. Chest CT demonstrated centrilobular nodular opacities. ¹⁸F-FDG-PET showed diffuse pulmonary uptake. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance of 12 Wood units.
reasoning_trace:
1. Acute coronary syndrome was excluded because “urgent catheterization showed no coronary stenosis…”  
2. Pulmonary embolism was excluded because “Emergent contrast-enhanced CT revealed no PE…”  
3. Aortic dissection was excluded because “Emergent contrast-enhanced CT revealed no … aortic dissection.”  
4. Asthma exacerbation or hypereosinophilic obliterative bronchiolitis was considered given the hypoxaemia and bronchiolitis-type CT features, but it was unresponsive to “2‐weeks of inhaled corticosteroid therapy.”  
5. Primary pulmonary arterial hypertension was considered but was unlikely given the combination of hypereosinophilia and diffuse pulmonary inflammation on ¹⁸F-FDG-PET rather than isolated vascular remodeling.

presentation: A 73-year-old woman presented with a painless, palpable mass in her right breast of more than 1 month’s duration. She had no B symptoms and no family history of breast cancer. On examination, there was a hard, 50 mm mass in the outer quadrant of the right breast without palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography showed a high-density mass with microlobulated margins. Ultrasonography revealed a 47 mm irregular hypoechoic mass with a heterogeneous internal echo and internal blood flow. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a solitary breast mass without evidence of metastases. MRI demonstrated that the margin of the mass was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; the time–intensity curve on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging showed a slow plateau pattern. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 15-3 were normal; lactate dehydrogenase was 207 IU/L. Core needle biopsy revealed solid proliferation of atypical cells with rounded nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining was negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2; the Ki67 labeling index was 80%. Based on these findings, the lesion was diagnosed as triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma (cT2N0M0).
reasoning_trace:
1. Initial diagnosis of triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma was made because “Analysis of a core needle biopsy (CNB) specimen revealed solid proliferation of atypical cells with rounded nuclei… the lesion was identified as invasive ductal carcinoma, solid type, nuclear grade 3… IHC staining showed that the tumor was negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and human epidermal growth factor 2.”  
2. Primary breast lymphoma (PBL) was considered due to MRI signal characteristics that are typical for lymphoma: “PBL is hyperintense on T2‐weighted images and isointense on T1‐weighted images… most PBLs display type 2 kinetic curves (slow or rapid enhancement and plateau in the delayed phase)… In our case, the MRI findings were consistent with the diagnosis of PBL.”  
3. The diagnosis was corrected to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma when immunohistochemical studies demonstrated B-cell markers: “IHC staining indicated positivity for leukocyte common antigen (LCA), CD20… Bcl‐6, and MUM‐1… Therefore, the diagnosis was corrected to DLBCL, nongerminal center type.”

presentation: A 37-year-old woman with no prior medical or surgical history presented with a 2-month history of progressive abdominal pain and distension, worsening fatigue, and an 8-kg weight loss. She denied fever or night sweats. On examination, she appeared cachectic; abdominal examination revealed dullness to percussion without tenderness or palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a leukocytosis, normal creatinine, and an elevated serum CA 125 level of 414.6 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated mild ascites of slightly high attenuation (38 HU) causing scalloping of the liver margins, omental fat stranding with nodular peritoneal thickening, and multiple mesenteric lymphadenopathies associated with diffuse thickening and enhancement of the small-bowel wall.
reasoning_trace:
1. Peritoneal carcinomatosis was considered because “peritoneal carcinomatosis of an ovarian epithelial carcinoma was the first-listed diagnosis” but was excluded after biopsy showed “no histopathological evidence of malignancy.”  
2. Pseudomyxoma peritonei was considered due to scalloping of the liver margins and peritoneal fluid but was less likely because “the presence of a fluid or soft tissue mass on the appendix is highly suggestive” and such a mass was not noted.  
3. Peritoneal lymphoma was considered given mesenteric lymphadenopathies but was unlikely as it is “characterized by bulky, non-obstructing, homogenously enhanced, masses encasing the mesenteric vasculature, featuring the ‘sandwich’ sign,” which was not present.  
4. Peritoneal tuberculosis was ultimately diagnosed after histology revealed caseating granulomas consistent with tuberculosis infection.

presentation:
A 10-year-old boy presented with a slowly progressive deformity of the right ankle. He had sustained a foot injury at age 5, which caused medial ankle pain and limping, treated by unknown orthopedic measures. Over time, a varus deformity and medial swelling of the right ankle developed. On examination, there was swelling on the medial aspect of the right ankle with marked varus alignment of the foot, limited ankle motion, and an antalgic gait. Palpation elicited severe pain over the medial tibio-talar joint. The remainder of the musculoskeletal and systemic examination was unremarkable.

A standard radiograph of the right ankle demonstrated an exophytic, intra-articularly oriented bony mass arising from the anteromedial aspects of the distal tibial epiphysis and the talus.

A CT scan with multiplanar reconstructions revealed multiple epiphyseal osteocartilaginous outgrowths—some pedunculated, others broad-based—arising from the medial portions of the talar epiphysis, navicular, medial cuneiform, and inferomedial tibial epiphysis, with extension into and adjacent to the talocalcaneal and talonavicular joints.
reasoning_trace:
1. Considered osteochondroma — “distinct in the epiphyseal location in the case of HED and metaphyseal location in the case of osteochondroma.”  
2. Considered multiple hereditary exostosis — “the risk of multiple hereditary exostosis degeneration into chondrosarcoma is possible and is nil in the case of HED.”  
3. Considered synovial chondromatosis — “with a normal aspect of the epiphysis, which differentiates it from the HED.”  
4. Considered myositis ossificans — “calcification in soft tissues (muscles, tendons, and fascia) without bone involvement, which differentiates it from HED.”  
5. Considered tumoral calcinosis — “without involvement of the adjacent joint, the epiphysis appears normal, which is not the case in HED.”  
6. Considered vascular or parasitic calcifications — “which can sometimes be mistaken for a HED lesion given the presentation as periarticular swelling.”  
7. Considered Ollier’s disease — “there is no hemimelic localization of the lesions, which differentiates it from HED.”  
8. Considered Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — “The cyclic evolution of this pathology definitely supports the diagnosis.”  
9. Considered capsular or para-articular chondroma — “the lesion is not related to the epiphysis. This appearance helps to differentiate it from HED.”

presentation:
A middle-aged man with no prior medical history presented with a 3-day history of intense throbbing headache (9/10), high fever up to 40.6 °C, and diffuse limb aches. He had no photophobia, phonophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, or meningeal signs. Neurologic and general physical examinations were unremarkable. He denied recent travel, animal exposures, gardening, or new medications.
